LIFE INSURANCE BENEFICIARY DESIGNATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Life Insurance Co.

POLICY OWNER, INSURER, AND BENEFICIARY DECLARATION
Jordan Alex Lee is the owner of a life insurance policy, policy number LI-1234567, issued by Acme Life Insurance Co. Jordan Alex Lee intends to designate Taylor Morgan as primary beneficiary under the policy. If Riley Chen is also named, Taylor Morgan and Riley Chen are both named as primary beneficiaries, to receive the policy's proceeds in equal shares if both survive Jordan Alex Lee, unless Jordan Alex Lee instead directs Acme Life Insurance Co. in writing to use different shares. Casey Rivera is named as contingent beneficiary, to receive the policy's proceeds only if no primary beneficiary survives Jordan Alex Lee. This designation is intended to be revocable. This declaration records Jordan Alex Lee's intended beneficiary designation for Jordan Alex Lee's own planning purposes; it does not, by itself, change or create a legally effective beneficiary designation on the policy. A beneficiary designation becomes legally effective only when it is reflected in the beneficiary designation form or other policy document that Acme Life Insurance Co. itself uses to record it.

LIFE INSURANCE AS A NONPROBATE TRANSFER BY WRITTEN INSTRUMENT
California's Probate Code addresses this directly, not as an aside. Prob. Code § 5000(a) provides that a written instrument's provision for a nonprobate transfer at Jordan Alex Lee's death is not invalid merely because the instrument doesn't comply with the requirements for executing a will — and the statute names an insurance policy specifically as one kind of instrument this covers, alongside things like a trust, a deed of gift, and a revocable transfer on death deed. In other words, a beneficiary designation on a life insurance policy such as the one Jordan Alex Lee holds with Acme Life Insurance Co. (policy number LI-1234567) is one of the statute's own named examples of a California-recognized nonprobate transfer: on Jordan Alex Lee's death, the policy's proceeds are paid according to the beneficiary designation on file with Acme Life Insurance Co., without going through probate and without that designation itself needing to satisfy will-execution formalities like witnesses. This Probate Code provision validates that kind of arrangement generally; it is a separate question — addressed elsewhere in this document — what specifically authorizes and governs the mechanics of naming, and later changing, a beneficiary under a particular life insurance policy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A provision for a nonprobate transfer on death in an insurance policy, contract of employment, bond, mortgage, promissory note, certificated or uncertificated security, account agreement, custodial agreement, deposit agreement, compensation plan, pension plan, individual retirement plan, employee benefit plan, trust, conveyance, deed of gift, revocable transfer on death deed, marital property agreement, or other written instrument of a similar nature is not invalid because the instrument does not comply with the requirements for execution of a will, and this code does not invalidate the instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5000(a), California Probate Code, nonprobate transfer by written instrument, naming an insurance policy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5000.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about what any particular reader should name as a beneficiary or do with their own policy. Prob. Code § 5000 is Probate Code Division 5's general nonprobate-transfer provision; it sits alongside, and does not replace, the separate scheme in the Insurance Code that regulates the life-insurance beneficiary-designation mechanism itself (addressed in this document's next clause). This is a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was located or needed to confirm this specific enumeration.

SOURCE OF THE BENEFICIARY-DESIGNATION MECHANISM, AND ITS REVOCABILITY
The specific power that lets Jordan Alex Lee name Taylor Morgan as beneficiary under the policy Jordan Alex Lee holds with Acme Life Insurance Co., and later change that designation, comes from the policy itself — not from a Probate Code command dictating who must be named. Cal. Ins. Code § 10170(e) makes this explicit: the terms and restrictions governing revocation by the policyholder, and control by beneficiaries, are those "agreed to in writing by the insurer and the policyholder" (or, if the insurer and policyholder never agreed to terms during Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime, those later agreed to in writing by the insurer and the beneficiaries). The same subdivision then supplies the default rule for how those terms can be undone: an agreement — including its terms on revocation — may generally be rescinded or amended by the parties to it without Taylor Morgan's consent, unless Taylor Morgan's rights have been expressly declared irrevocable, in which case that consent is required to change the designation. So the beneficiary-designation mechanism itself is fundamentally a matter of the insurance contract; what the Insurance Code supplies is the background default rule about when a beneficiary's consent is, and is not, required to change it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Upon those terms and conditions and subject to those restrictions as to revocation by the policyholder and control by beneficiaries as shall have been agreed to in writing by the insurer and the policyholder. If no terms and conditions have been agreed to by the insurer and the policyholder during the insured’s lifetime then upon those terms and conditions and subject to those restrictions as may be agreed to in writing by the insurer and the beneficiaries. Any agreement may be rescinded or amended by the parties to the agreement without the consent of any designated beneficiary unless the rights of any beneficiary have been expressly declared to be irrevocable."
  — Cal. Ins. Code § 10170(e), California Insurance Code, terms of revocation and control by beneficiaries; irrevocable-beneficiary consent rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=INS&sectionNum=10170.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about whether any particular policy owner should designate a beneficiary as revocable or irrevocable. Cal. Ins. Code § 10170 has several lettered subdivisions describing the different ways life insurance may be made payable; only subdivision (e), which supplies the revocation and irrevocable-consent rule, is quoted here. This is a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was located for it. Separately, this section describes what California's default statutory framework permits the policy to say — it does not itself state what any specific insurer's policy form actually provides, which controls in practice and can vary by insurer and by policy.

COMMUNITY PROPERTY PREMIUMS AND A BENEFICIARY OTHER THAN THE OWNER'S SPOUSE
If Jordan Alex Lee is married, and premiums on the policy with Acme Life Insurance Co. were paid using community property funds, naming someone other than Jordan Alex Lee's spouse as Taylor Morgan intersects with California's community property law in a way this document flags rather than resolves. Two separate statutes bear on it. First, Fam. Code § 1100(b) provides that a spouse "may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the written consent of the other spouse" — and naming a non-spouse as the beneficiary of a policy funded with community property premiums can be treated as this kind of disposition. Second, Prob. Code § 5011 provides that the rights of the parties in a nonprobate transfer of community property on death — a category that, per this document's first clause, expressly includes a life insurance policy — are subject to the terms of the instrument, any contrary statute specifically applicable to it, and a written expression of intent or consent by a party. Neither statute, on its own text, announces a single fixed outcome for every such policy; together they establish that a non-owner spouse's community property interest in a policy is a real, statutorily-recognized issue when the named beneficiary isn't that spouse, not something a beneficiary designation alone necessarily overrides. What community property and quasi-community property mean under California law generally is addressed elsewhere in this corpus's community property materials.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the written consent of the other spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(b), California Family Code, spousal consent required for a gift of community personal property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1100.)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, the rights of the parties in a nonprobate transfer of community property on death are subject to all of the following: (a) The terms of the instrument under which the nonprobate transfer is made. (b) A contrary state statute specifically applicable to the instrument under which the nonprobate transfer is made. (c) A written expression of intent of a party in the provision for transfer of the property or in a written consent to the provision."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5011, California Probate Code, rights of parties in a nonprobate transfer of community property on death (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5011.)
  Known gap: This is California's law, used as evidence of what California statutes provide — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's marriage or policy, and not advice about whether any specific policy, premium history, or beneficiary designation does or does not require a spouse's consent. Fam. Code § 1100(b) and Prob. Code § 5011 are separate statutes in different codes, each independently retrieved and verified — not subsections of the same section. California case law bearing specifically on a non-owner spouse's interest in a life insurance policy naming a third party — the kind of authority one might expect alongside these statutes — could not be verified this session: the case-law research tool available for this task returned a rate-limit error (daily quota exhausted) before any case could be retrieved and confirmed, so no case citation is included here; that gap is disclosed rather than filled with an unverified case. This clause relies on, rather than re-derives, this corpus's own existing statutory definition of community and quasi-community property.

SIMULTANEOUS DEATH OF THE INSURED AND A BENEFICIARY
California has a default rule specifically for a life insurance beneficiary who dies at the same time as the insured, or where it can't be established by clear and convincing evidence which of them survived the other — and it is not the 120-hour survival rule that governs wills and intestate succession. Under Prob. Code § 224, if it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that Taylor Morgan survived Jordan Alex Lee as the insured, the policy's proceeds are administered as if Jordan Alex Lee survived Taylor Morgan — meaning Taylor Morgan's designation is treated as though it lapsed — except that if the policy is community or quasi-community property of Jordan Alex Lee and Jordan Alex Lee's spouse, and there is no other named beneficiary besides Jordan Alex Lee's own estate or personal representative, the proceeds are instead distributed as community property under a separate statute. This default rule has real limits on when it applies: under Prob. Code § 221, this chapter's simultaneous-death rules do not apply at all if the policy or a related agreement contains its own explicit provision addressing simultaneous deaths, a common-disaster clause, or a stated survival period different from what this default rule provides — so a policy or beneficiary form that speaks to the issue directly controls instead of this default.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the insured and a beneficiary under a policy of life or accident insurance have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that the beneficiary survived the insured, the proceeds of the policy shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if the insured had survived the beneficiary, except if the policy is community or quasi-community property of the insured and the spouse of the insured and there is no alternative beneficiary except the estate or personal representative of the insured, the proceeds shall be distributed as community property under Section 103."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 224, California Probate Code, simultaneous death of insured and beneficiary under a life or accident policy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=224.)
  "This chapter does not apply in the case of a trust, deed, or contract of insurance, or any other situation, where (1) provision is made dealing explicitly with simultaneous deaths or deaths in a common disaster or otherwise providing for distribution of property different from the provisions of this chapter or (2) provision is made requiring one person to survive another for a stated period in order to take property or providing for a presumption as to survivorship that results in a distribution of property different from that provided by this chapter."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 221(b), California Probate Code, chapter inapplicable where the policy addresses simultaneous death itself (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=221.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a life insurance beneficiary specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about how a specific policy's own survivorship language should be drafted or interpreted. Prob. Code § 224 and § 221 are separate, independently retrieved and verified statutory sections within the same chapter of the Probate Code (the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act as adopted in California) — they are treated as independent sources of what each provides, not as subsections of one section, though both come from the same statutory chapter. This clause does not address the separate 120-hour survival requirement that Prob. Code § 6403 applies to wills and intestate succession; § 221(a) itself provides that this chapter does not apply where § 6403 (among other sections) applies, so the two default rules are not interchangeable, and this document does not assume the 120-hour rule extends to a life insurance beneficiary designation.

A BENEFICIARY WHO FELONIOUSLY AND INTENTIONALLY KILLS THE INSURED
California's slayer statute reaches a life insurance beneficiary specifically, not only a probate or intestate heir. Prob. Code § 252 provides that a named beneficiary of a bond, life insurance policy, or other contractual arrangement who feloniously and intentionally kills the person on whose life the policy is issued is not entitled to any benefit under it, and the policy becomes payable as though the killer had predeceased the insured — so if Taylor Morgan feloniously and intentionally killed Jordan Alex Lee as the insured, Taylor Morgan forfeits the designation under this statute regardless of what the policy's own paperwork says. This isn't limited to that dedicated life-insurance provision: the general slayer-disqualification statute, Prob. Code § 250(a)(4), separately disqualifies a feloniously-and-intentionally-killing beneficiary from "any property of the decedent under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000)" — the same Probate Code division that, as described elsewhere in this document, expressly includes a life insurance policy's nonprobate transfer provision — confirming the slayer rule isn't confined to wills and intestate succession. How the killing itself gets established for these purposes is addressed by Prob. Code § 254: a final criminal conviction for the felonious and intentional killing is conclusive, and without one, a court may find it by a preponderance of the evidence, with the burden on whoever is asserting the disqualification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A named beneficiary of a bond, life insurance policy, or other contractual arrangement who feloniously and intentionally kills the principal obligee or the person upon whose life the policy is issued is not entitled to any benefit under the bond, policy, or other contractual arrangement, and it becomes payable as though the killer had predeceased the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 252, California Probate Code, slayer disqualification for a named life insurance beneficiary (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=252.)
  "Any property of the decedent under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 250(a)(4), California Probate Code, general slayer statute's cross-reference to Division 5 nonprobate transfers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=250.)
  "A final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing is conclusive for purposes of this part. (b) In the absence of a final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing, the court may determine by a preponderance of evidence whether the killing was felonious and intentional for purposes of this part. The burden of proof is on the party seeking to establish that the killing was felonious and intentional for the purposes of this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 254(a)-(b), California Probate Code, how a felonious and intentional killing is established (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=254.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about, or a finding regarding, whether any actual beneficiary of any actual policy has committed a disqualifying act; whether a specific killing was "felonious and intentional" within the meaning of this statute is a fact-specific determination for a court, as § 254 itself describes, not something this document resolves. Prob. Code §§ 252, 250(a)(4), and 254 are three separate, independently retrieved and verified statutory sections; § 250(a)(4) is quoted only for its cross-reference to Division 5, not for the full list of interests it disqualifies.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
SIGNATURE AND DATE: Jordan Alex Lee signs and dates this declaration below.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: _________________________ Date: _______________

Printed name: _________________________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT: Jordan Alex Lee understands that this declaration is a planning worksheet reflecting Jordan Alex Lee's intended beneficiary designation for the policy numbered LI-1234567 with Acme Life Insurance Co., and that it does not itself change or bind any beneficiary designation on file with Acme Life Insurance Co. Jordan Alex Lee understands that to make the designation legally effective, Jordan Alex Lee must separately complete Acme Life Insurance Co.'s own beneficiary designation form, and that Acme Life Insurance Co. may require government-issued identification, an original signature, or additional paperwork of its own choosing before doing so. Jordan Alex Lee further understands that, unless the designation has been made irrevocable with Taylor Morgan's consent, the designation can generally be changed during Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime by submitting a new designation to Acme Life Insurance Co. in the form and manner Acme Life Insurance Co. requires.

NOTARIZATION NOTICE: California law does not require this declaration to be notarized or witnessed to be effective; what governs is the beneficiary designation actually on file with Acme Life Insurance Co. This declaration is kept for Jordan Alex Lee's own records, alongside a copy of the designation paperwork Acme Life Insurance Co. provides.
